# Voyage to the Blue Planet
Voyage to the Blue Planet was a 2024 concert tour by the American rock band Weezer. Staged in North America to commemorate the 30th anniversary of Weezer’s 1994 self-titled debut album (known as the “Blue Album”), the tour ran from early September to mid-October 2024. On this tour, the band performed the Blue Album in its entirety, along with a selection of other hits and fan-favorite songs from their catalog. Produced by Live Nation and sponsored by Citi, Voyage to the Blue Planet included performances in major arenas across the United States and Canada. The shows featured support from fellow alternative rock bands The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr., who served as opening acts throughout the tour. Notably, the concert production embraced an elaborate outer space theme: Weezer’s members donned astronaut-style jumpsuits and acted out a lighthearted sci-fi narrative in which they travel to a “Blue Planet” and save it through the power of music. The tour received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its playful camp aesthetic and the band’s energetic performance of their classic material.
## Background and Development
In late 2023, Weezer began hinting that they had special plans to celebrate the Blue Album’s 30th anniversary. Frontman Rivers Cuomo revealed in a December 2023 interview that the band was preparing “a really amazing deluxe package with a bunch of additional material” for the album and “of course, we’ve gotta do some kind of epic tour” to mark the milestone. He noted that while the band hadn’t staged a major commemoration for the album’s 20th anniversary, they intended to “give it its due respect” at 30 years. By early 2024, further clues began to emerge. On February 28, 2024, Weezer launched a cryptic website (BlueVoyage2024.com) and social media teaser with the message, “Are you prepared for the voyage?” – showing the band in what looked like space suits – and declaring that “the voyage takes flight on March 11, 2024”. This led to widespread speculation that an space-themed Blue Album anniversary tour was imminent.
On March 11, 2024, Weezer officially announced the Voyage to the Blue Planet Tour, confirming it as an extensive North American arena tour celebrating 30 years of the Blue Album. The tour was scheduled to kick off on September 4, 2024, at the Xcel Energy Center in Saint Paul, Minnesota, and to conclude on October 11, 2024, at the new Intuit Dome in Inglewood, California. (A final show on October 12 in Palm Springs was later added as the tour finale.) As promised, the band would perform the entire Blue Album front-to-back at each show, in addition to “other fan favorites, rarities and more” from their discography. The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr. were announced as special guests and opening acts for all dates. Tickets went on sale mid-March, with presales via the band’s mailing list and Citi (the tour’s official credit card sponsor). Weezer also arranged a separate one-off anniversary event on March 15, 2024 (months before the tour) at a small venue in Los Angeles, where they performed the Blue Album in full with special guests – a nod to the band’s early club days.
## Concert Production and Synopsis
Weezer performing in astronaut attire during the Voyage to the Blue Planet tour, 2024.
Each Voyage to the Blue Planet concert was presented as a tongue-in-cheek space adventure, complete with theatrical props, themed visuals, and a loose storyline connecting the songs. The stage design featured a retro-styled rocket ship at center stage and scenery made to resemble an extraterrestrial landscape – including fake “space rocks” (asteroid props) scattered around. At the start of the show, a countdown clock appeared on the screens, mimicking a spacecraft launch sequence. When the countdown reached zero, the on-stage “rocket” dramatically lifted up amid sparklers and smoke, revealing the band members beneath it in full astronaut-like jumpsuits. Amid cheers from the audience, Weezer opened the show by launching into the first song as if “taking off” on their voyage.
Throughout the concert, large video screens and special effects helped tell the story of Weezer’s journey through space. The band “traveled” from Earth toward the distant Blue Planet (a symbolic reference to their Blue Album and the planet Earth) and encountered various cosmic scenes that tied in with their music. For example, at times inflatable planets and UFO models would descend from the arena ceiling, and a giant circular screen at the back of the stage displayed animated outer-space imagery to simulate the voyage. Visual cues referencing the band’s album colors and themes were woven into the set: when a red planet hovered above the stage, Weezer launched into songs from their “Red Album,” and when green visuals appeared, they played a track from the “Green Album” (“Hash Pipe”). During the pop hit “Beverly Hills,” neon palm trees flashed on screen (a playful nod to the song’s subject), while old-fashioned television sets floated by during the mellow tune “Any Friend of Diane’s”.
The concert’s narrative found the band confronted by a campy alien antagonist as they ventured deeper into space. Midway through the set, a talking CGI creature (displayed on the screen) informed Rivers Cuomo that their spaceship had become stranded in an asteroid field. “What asteroid belt?” Cuomo asked in mock confusion, to which the creature replied, “Why, the Pinkerton Asteroid Belt, of course!”. This tongue-in-cheek moment drew cheers from the crowd, as it signaled the band would now play songs from Pinkerton (Weezer’s 1996 second album) as the next part of the show. Indeed, the band then performed a medley of five Pinkerton-era songs – including “Getchoo,” “Why Bother?,” and “Pink Triangle” – to represent their traversal through the so-called Pinkerton Asteroid Belt. During this segment the show’s “plot” had the spaceship damaged by the alien enemy (nicknamed “Bokkus” in the show’s script) and crash-landing before reaching its destination. The thematic gag offered a fun way to include a sampling of Pinkerton tracks, adding some heavier and more abrasive songs to the set before the main event.
After escaping the asteroid belt, Weezer finally “arrived” at the Blue Planet – setting the stage for the highlight of the night: a complete performance of the Blue Album. In the show’s narrative, the Blue Planet was in peril of destruction, and the only way to save it was for the band to play their debut album in full. Rivers Cuomo announced to the crowd that the mission had reached its crucial moment and delivered a cheeky line: “One small step for Weezer, one giant leap for Weezer-kind,” parodying Neil Armstrong as they prepared to launch into the album’s opening track. The band members planted a blue-colored flag with Weezer’s “W” logo on the stage to signify their landing on the planet. They then proceeded to perform every song from Weezer (The Blue Album) (1994) in its original sequence, from “My Name Is Jonas” through “Only in Dreams.” The audience enthusiastically sang along to these classic tracks; during hits like “Buddy Holly” and “Say It Ain’t So,” the entire arena joined in chorus. In an especially interactive moment on “Undone – The Sweater Song,” the band dropped out during the chorus to let the crowd shout the lyrics unaccompanied. Blue-colored lighting and confetti effects heightened the atmosphere—blue streamers rained down and the venue was bathed in blue light as the album reached its climax. At the finale of “Only in Dreams,” cannons shot out bursts of blue confetti (dubbed “stardust”) over the cheering crowd.
Weezer largely stuck to the music with minimal between-song chatter, adhering to the playful “space mission” script for most of the night. Near the end, Rivers Cuomo broke character briefly to marvel at the sight of fans starting a mosh pit during the normally slow-burning “Only in Dreams,” joking that he’d “never seen a mosh pit for that song in 30 years”. After finishing the Blue Album set, the band took their bows “and left the planet” – exiting the stage as the storyline’s mission was fulfilled. They thanked their “flight crew” (the touring staff and crew), the opening bands, and the fans before making their final exit to an outro video (a humorous “post-credits scene” played on-screen to cap off the space adventure). The entire performance ran roughly 90–100 minutes and featured about 30 songs spanning Weezer’s career, making for a full evening of music wrapped in a whimsical sci-fi presentation.
## Critical Reception
Voyage to the Blue Planet was met with broadly positive reception from both critics and audiences, who appreciated the tour’s balance of nostalgia, showmanship, and musicality. Reviewers frequently noted that the concert’s deliberately campy science-fiction motif added a fun, theatrical twist to what could have simply been a standard 30th-anniversary set. Rolling Stone described the Blue Album anniversary show as “glorious sci-fi camp,” observing that Weezer embraced an outlandishly ridiculous space-opera concept while still delivering their songs with serious skill. The band’s performance was consistently strong: the members have “been playing together for decades” and moved through the complex setlist “seamlessly with little chatter,” commented the Boston Globe, which praised Weezer as “so brilliantly cohesive as a band” and noted that their multi-generational fans responded with joy at every turn. Many critics highlighted the complete run-through of the Blue Album as the emotional high point of the night, citing the electric crowd sing-alongs to hits like “Buddy Holly,” “Say It Ain’t So,” and “Undone – The Sweater Song” as evidence of the album’s enduring appeal. Chris Stevens of Boston.com wrote that “you couldn’t help but get caught up in the rush and the thrash and the joy of it all” during the finale, given how beloved those songs are to the fanbase.
The tour’s extravagant staging also drew commentary. Variety noted that the galactic set pieces and costumes verged on the silly side – one reviewer quipped that by the time dancing aliens and planets were flying around, the show felt “a bit like watching the Wiggles… only with louder guitars” – yet most critics understood that the campiness was intentional and part of the entertainment. Several reviews pointed out that few bands of Weezer’s stature would attempt such a quirky, self-deprecating concept for an arena rock show, and that Weezer’s willingness to poke fun at themselves made the concerts endearing. Wayne Coyne of The Flaming Lips (one of the opening acts) gave the production a strong endorsement on opening night, calling the show “effing mind-blowing” from the stage. Publications like Rolling Stone and Kerrang! emphasized that the “Voyage” tour successfully turned Weezer’s nostalgia for 1994 into an imaginative spectacle rather than a straightforward nostalgia trip. Overall, the consensus was that Voyage to the Blue Planet provided a highly enjoyable experience: a celebration of a classic album delivered with a mix of sincere musical reverence and tongue-in-cheek theatrics. Even some initially skeptical commentators admitted that the concept paid off. As one radio reviewer put it, “there’s a really cool story that takes place throughout the show…even if you’re a passive Weezer fan I highly recommend it – it’s a really fun experience”.
## Concert Film and Recordings
Recognizing the demand from fans beyond the tour stops, Weezer documented the Voyage to the Blue Planet show for posterity. On September 10, 2024, the band’s performance at TD Garden in Boston was professionally filmed with a full multi-camera setup. The footage from that night was edited into a live concert film titled “Weezer’s Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film.” The band announced that the film would be released as a special streaming event: it was broadcast online via the Moment House platform on October 13 and 14, 2024, while the tour was still ongoing. In a social media teaser for the film, Weezer jokingly referenced the moon landing quote and invited fans who “couldn’t make it out to the tour” to join the Voyage from home. The concert film captures the full live show, including the Blue Album performance and all the space-themed theatrics, allowing viewers to experience the narrative arc of the concert. Early-bird tickets for the streaming premiere were offered, and the film was later made available for on-demand viewing for a limited time.
In addition to the concert film, the band’s 30th anniversary celebrations included an expansive reissue of the Blue Album. In November 2024, Weezer released a deluxe 30th-anniversary edition of Weezer (Blue Album) featuring dozens of previously unreleased demos and outtakes. This reissue was timed to coincide with the end of the tour, giving fans new archival material from the same era that the tour was commemorating. While no live album from the Voyage to the Blue Planet tour has been released, the streaming concert film effectively serves as its official live document. The film and the tour as a whole were seen as a fitting tribute to the Blue Album’s legacy – combining live nostalgia with an inventive, light-hearted twist that underscored Weezer’s unique personality as a band.

[Concert Reviews](https://www.boston.com/tag/concert-reviews/)

Opening acts Dinosaur Jr. & The Flaming Lips left their marks Tuesday night as well.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 1](https://bdc2020.o0bc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/s3___bgmp-arc_arc-feeds_generic-photos_to-arc_12weezer-13-66e1a13e41c9a-768x432.jpg)

Singer/guitarist Rivers Cuomo performs with Weezer at TD Garden Tuesday night. _Ben Stas for The Boston Globe_

#### Share

Send this article to your social connections.

**_Weezer, with Dinosaur Jr. and The Flaming Lips, TD Garden, Sept. 10, 2024_**

When Wayne Coyne, lead singer of opening band The Flaming Lips, said Weezer’s “Voyage to the Blue Planet” show was “effing mind blowing,” he was not wrong.

To call it otherworldly wouldn’t even be hyperbole, since the NASA-esque jumpsuit-suited band materialized on the TD Garden stage Tuesday night as their spacecraft lifted off, leaving behind swirling white clouds. At the same time, they launched the audience on what lead singer/guitarist Rivers Cuomo called a “very dangerous mission.”

It was all camp, all fun, and everyone was all-in as the alt-rock band played out the space-themed odyssey that included traveling 30 light years away to save the Blue Planet — by celebrating their Blue Album, [released 30 years ago](https://weezer.com/news/2024/9/4/30th-anniversary-of-the-blue-album-box-sets-tour-amp-more). The space party was set in motion when breaking news announced an imminent space voyage, and a countdown clock ticked off the band’s liftoff, the heady crowd counting it down in unison.

The mood was enhanced by planets large and small that dropped into and out of the concert’s hemisphere. The stage was littered with space rocks and backed by a giant porthole that showed the band’s journey through space via special effects, to a wonderful degree of success. Pink palm trees flashed by when they launched into the always-a-crowd-pleaser “Beverly Hills,” and TVs floated past when they sang “Any Friend of Diane’s is a Friend of Mine.” And there was plenty of space stuff too.

The band moved through the music seamlessly with little chatter, like they’d been playing together for decades, which they have been.

And the clues baked in to the eras-spanning tour — not to be confused with that [other Eras Tour](https://www.boston.com/culture/entertainment/2023/10/16/taylor-swifts-eras-tour-no-1-box-office-eyeing-joker-film-record/) — were not lost on the crowd. When a red planet appeared at the start of the first set, the crowd knew what to expect and roared when the band launched into “Troublemaker,” from the Red Album, then flowed into the Green album for “Hashpipe,” and back to Red for “Pork and Beans.”

Bass player Scott Shriner started the show playing a translucent double-necked bass that was totally (inter)stellar. He and Cuomo and guitarist/vocalist Brian Bell traded riffs and shredding duties effortlessly, often lining up, playing in synch (but not NSYNC, to be clear) while Patrick Wilson kept perfect time and was often a blur on drums.

Hands double-tapped in the air all over the arena for “Island in the Sun,” before a spacecraft-flying CGI creature told Cuomo they were stranded in an asteroid belt.

“What asteroid belt?” Cuomo asked. “Why, the Pinkerton Asteroid Belt of course,” was the response, which set off a chain reaction of cheers across the arena as the band hurled into “Why Bother,” off what else but the “Pinkerton” album.

Midway through the show, Cuomo announced they’d arrived at the Blue Planet but they needed to perform the Blue Album to save it from certain destruction. It was the set everyone had clearly been wildly anticipating.

“One small step for Weezer, one giant leap for Weezer-kind,” Cuomo said before they jumped into the album’s opening track “My Name is Jonas,” followed up by “No One Else” and, of course, “Buddy Holly.”

(If you want to see the quartet talk about their iconic Blue Album and how the songs came to be, stop by [Weezer Live/Spotify THIRTY on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P_vI3FV1H4U), it’s a fun watch.)

Cuomo then admitted he was actually an alien (and so are all of you, he told the raucous sea of fans), and when he followed that up with “Undone – The Sweater Song,” he was matched lyric for lyric by a whipped-up crowd that couldn’t wait for more. In fact, the crowd pretty much took over for “Say It Ain’t So,” but it couldn’t drown out Bell’s screaming guitar solo.

Cuomo only seemed to step away from the space-themed scripted repartee of the show when a bit of crowd surfing broke out during “Only In Dreams.”

“In 30 years that’s the first time I’ve seen a mosh pit for that song,” he said.

![Image 2](https://bdc2020.o0bc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/s3___bgmp-arc_arc-feeds_generic-photos_to-arc_12weezer-9-66e1a77279213-scaled.jpg)

Guitarist Brian Bell, left, and singer/guitarist Rivers Cuomo perform with Weezer at TD Garden. _Ben Stas for The Boston Globe_

The music built to a chest-pounding crescendo as confetti cannons fired blue bits of stardust that hung in the air as the crowd chanted “Weezer, Weezer,” and they took a bow and left the planet, but not before thanking their flight crew, opening bands, and the fans.

##### More Reviews:

*   [#### Review & setlist: Green Day celebrates two albums at Fenway Park](https://www.boston.com/culture/concert-reviews/2024/08/08/review-setlist-green-day-celebrates-two-albums-at-fenway-park/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feature)
*   [#### Review & setlist: Gin Blossoms and Toad The Wet Sprocket have aged jangly](https://www.boston.com/culture/concert-reviews/2024/08/14/review-setlist-gin-blossoms-and-toad-the-wet-sprocket-have-aged-jangly/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feed)
*   [#### Review & setlist: Blink-182 refuse to act their age at Fenway Park](https://www.boston.com/culture/concert-reviews/2024/07/25/blink-182-fenway-park-boston-concert-review-setlist/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feed)

As much fun as the goofy setting amid some serious music was, the best thing about the show was the fact that Weezer is undeniably fun — so brilliantly cohesive as a band and loyal to their music and their fans. And their fans, from the very young wearing noise canceling headphones to the teens and tweens (wasn’t that a school night?) dancing along with mom and dad, to the older fans also swaying and yelling lyrics into the atmosphere — they gave the love right back. You couldn’t help but get caught up in the rush and the thrash and the joy of it all.

Weezer fans were just as appreciative of the opening acts as well, each of which was met with the familiarity of head bobbing and sing-alongs.

For Dinosaur Jr., playing the Garden was a homecoming. The Amherst, Massachusetts, band was an interesting pairing for Weezer, with its hard-driving, psychedelic, ear-splitting set. To the woman two rows in front who handed me a pair of earplugs halfway through the set — I love you. They played a loud, proud, and tight 30 minutes with little chatter, save an intro and a good-bye. But J Mascis spoke plenty with his guitar shredding, as did Murph on drums and bass player Lou Barlow, who crashed about the stage, never standing still for more than a few seconds.

The Flaming Lips brought their own sense of camp, with inflatables and a laser light show that should have come with a “could induce seizures” warning.  Coyne admitted they were a little out of their element, having never played a venue as big as TD Garden, but Boston was not unfamiliar to them. He rattled off a list of memorable spots they gigged at over the years, including The Rat, T.T. the Bears, Middle East, Paradise Lounge, The Orpheum, and, just last year, [Boston Calling](https://www.boston.com/culture/music/2024/05/27/boston-calling-2024-festival-review/).

A divinely lush, yet also amped up and slightly magical version of Madonna’s “Borderline” was a standout for the band, but it was “She Don’t Use Jelly” and the “Yeah, Yeah, Yeah” song that got the crowd singing along and head-banging in time with two ginormous inflated pink robots and a couple of large eyeballs.

The Flaming Lips ended their set with Coyne encouraging folks to turn to the one they came with or the stranger next to them and tell them they love them, before launching into “Do You Realize,” which he sang standing under a blow-up rainbow.

Shout-out to the stranger next to me who assured me he loved me. Right back at you — and at Weezer too. How could you not after a Voyage to the Blue Planet?

On this anniversary tour produced by Live Nation, Weezer will be joined by The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr. as support.

Fans can sign up for Weezer’s mailing list to get access to presale tickets on Wednesday, March 13 at 12:00PM local time. More presales including a Citi presale (details below) will run throughout the week ahead of the general onsale beginning on Friday, March 15 at 10:00AM local time. For complete presale details visit [www.citientertainment.com.](https://www.citientertainment.com/)

Separate from their tour, the band also announced a special anniversary event on March 15th at the Lodge Room in Los Angeles with Dogstar as support. This exciting full-circle moment mirrors the band’s March 1992 show at Raji’s where they ended up opening for Dogstar in an unlikely turn of events. The name “Weezer” was coined in a conversation with the show’s booker. They will be playing Weezer (the Blue Album) front to back alongside some very special guests.

The run of dates kicks off in Saint Paul, Minnesota at the Xcel Energy Center on September 4th before traveling to major cities including Toronto, Boston, New York, Nashville, and Washington, D.C. to name a few. An instantly recognizable cultural touchstone of the 1990s, _Weezer_ (the Blue Album) has garnered such a firm place in the musical pantheon of the last three decades that it serves as an entry point into music for nascent listeners. **About Weezer:**

Weezer is an American rock band formed in Los Angeles, CA in 1992, currently consisting of Rivers Cuomo (lead vocals, lead guitar), Patrick Wilson (drums), Brian Bell (rhythm guitar, backing vocals, keyboards), and Scott Shriner (bass, backing vocals).  Weezer has sold 10 million albums in the U.S., and over 35 million records worldwide.  Their catalogue has included such megahits as “Buddy Holly,” “Undone (The Sweater Song),” “Say It Ain’t So,” “El Scorcho,” “Hash Pipe,” “Island In The Sun,” “Beverly Hills,” “Pork and Beans,” and more.   Weezer has won Grammys, MTV Video Music Awards, and more throughout their career.  Following massively acclaimed album releases in 2016 and 2017 (Weezer \[The White Album\] and Pacific Daydream, respectively), and two sold out amphitheater tours with Panic! At the Disco (in 2016) and Pixies (in 2018), Weezer released a fan-inspired cover of Toto’s “Africa.”  The cover propelled the band back into the charts across the board, giving Weezer their FIFTH #1, TENTH Top 5, and SIXTEENTH Top 10 at Alternative Radio, in addition to landing Top 5 on the Hot AC chart.   It has since gone Platinum.  They then surprise dropped a covers album at the start of 2019 — Weezer (The Teal Album) — which has been streamed over a hundred million times since its release.  In 2021, Weezer released two very different but equally Weezer albums – OK Human, an orchestral pop album meditating on technology and disconnectedness, and Van Weezer, an homage to the band’s shared metal roots growing up.  OK Human’s first single, “All My Favorite Songs,” was one of the biggest rock hits of 2021, and was subsequently nominated for a Grammy for “Best Rock Song.” In 2022, the band released SZNZ, a four EP project inspired by Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and completed the European leg of the Hella Mega tour, which sold out stadiums in America throughout the year prior. Photo: Getty Images North America

[**Weezer**](https://www.iheart.com/artist/weezer-15720/)'s 1994 debut _The Blue Album_ turned 30 next year, and the band is planning to celebrate it in epic fashion. **Rivers Cuomo** teased their big anniversary plans during a recent interview with [**_Collider_**](https://collider.com/weezer-blue-album-deluxe-edition-30th-anniversary-tour/).

“We are going to give it its due respect and come out with a really amazing deluxe package with a bunch of additional material, and of course, we’ve gotta do some kind of epic tour,” the frontman said after admitting they didn't give it a proper celebration for its 20th anniversary.

The band's on a UK tour with the [**Smashing Pumpkins**](https://www.iheart.com/artist/smashing-pumpkins-29249/) until June, but Cuomo pointed out that “there’s this very suspicious blank space in our calendar for months after that, so I’d keep your eye on that.”

Although Weezer didn't celebrate _The Blue Album_'s 20th anniversary, they did put out a deluxe version for its 10th anniversary in 2004. They also played it, along with _Pinkerton_, in its entirety during some shows in 2010.

In October, Cuomo checked something special off his bucket list: [**opening for KISS**](https://www.iheart.com/content/2023-10-09-weezer-just-played-a-show-they-could-never-have-dreamed-of/). "Thank you to the first band I ever fell in love with. It was an absolute dream come true," he gushed on social media at the time. Cuomo has made his [**love of metal**](https://www.iheart.com/content/2022-10-17-weezer-considered-playing-enter-sandman-at-festival-opening-for-metallica/) known over the years and was even in a [**metal band before starting Weezer**](https://www.iheart.com/content/2020-07-06-rivers-cuomo-was-in-a-metal-band-before-forming-weezer/).

Weezer’s Blue Album Tour Turns Their Hits Into Glorious Sci-Fi Camp
===================================================================

The alt-rock stars celebrate the 30th anniversary of their beloved debut in the best, most ridiculous way possible (plus opening sets from the Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr.)

By [Evan Minsker](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/evan-minsker/)

### [Evan Minsker](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/evan-minsker/)

September 5, 2024

![Image 2: ST PAUL, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 4: Rivers Cuomo of the band Weezer performs at Xcel Energy Center on September 4, 2024 in St Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

At one point in Weezer's tour kickoff in Saint Paul, Rivers Cuomo revealed that he was an alien from the Blue Planet. Adam Bettcher/Getty Images

There was at least some hubris in [Weezer](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/weezer/)’s 30th anniversary Blue Album tour announcement. Openers the [Flaming Lips](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/flaming-lips/) and [Dinosaur Jr.](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/dinosaur-jr/) are more than potential show-stealers, they’re established headliners in their own right. How do you follow that? You drop a giant curtain to reveal a Weezer-branded spacecraft. It seemed instantly clear at the tour opener in Saint Paul, Minn., on Sept. 4 that Weezer have reached new heights as an arena band.

After a countdown where an Xcel Energy Center full of voices screamed “5, 4, 3, 2, 1,” the vessel took flight into the rafters, leaving a trail of pyro in its wake. It revealed Weezer’s four members in NASA-esque jumpsuits gripping their instruments. The stage was covered in space boulders; periodically, small planets and UFOs would hover above their heads. A giant screen behind them showed a mission through the CGI stars. The narrative goes something like this: Sci-fi space heroes Weezer need to make it to the distant Blue Planet, which is facing an ecological crisis. The only solution is to travel there and perform the debut album they released 30 “lightyears” ago.

It’s a deeply goofy and campy premise, but which show do you want: a straightforward, buttoned-up, front-to-back full-album concert, or a ridiculous, Sixties-television-aping space opera featuring a Weezer concert? This show feels like the meeting point between the guided narrative of Disneyland’s _Star Tours_ and the rock & roll theatrics of an Iron Maiden show. At one point Rivers Cuomo, who had been shredding effortlessly through his greatest hits for over an hour, revealed that he was an alien from the Blue Planet. My guy literally did the _Muppets From Space_ plot. This is the Weezer arena show we want.

More than just fun and absurd scene-setting, the narrative guided a setlist that led gradually to the Blue Album. It’s savvy work, opening with songs like “Pork and Beans” and “Hash Pipe” instead of launching right into the Blue Album. Everybody came in expecting the full-album treatment, so to instead open with a mini-eras block was an invigorating surprise. And of course, all of the songs soundtracked some space-narrative CGI stuff on the jumbotron. Red Album songs were played as red planets whipped by on the screen behind them. “Island in the Sun,” in this tour’s context, is about an island literally inside a sun.

Editor’s picks
--------------

[![Image 3](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-albums-21st-century-1235177256/)

[![Image 4](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time](https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-lists/best-tv-episodes-of-all-time-1235090945/)

[![Image 5](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-albums-of-all-time-1062063/)

[![Image 6](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century](https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-lists/best-movies-of-the-21st-century-1235200512/)

“We are currently marooned in an asteroid belt,” a CGI robot told Rivers Cuomo. “Hmm,” he responded, “it looks familiar. Which asteroid belt?” After a beat, the robot replied, “The Pinkerton Asteroid Belt, of course.” The crowd howled as the stage was bathed in pink light. The band performed a block of _Pinkerton_ songs including “Why Bother?” and “Pink Triangle.” Weezer’s playing was airtight. The performances were exceptional throughout the set, guitar solos and vocal harmonies hitting just right every single time. It’s impressive how this band can stay so faithful to their source material decades into their tenure.

![Image 7](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Weezer and their spaceship in Saint Paul (from left, Patrick Wilson, Brian Bell, Rivers Cuomo, and Scott Shriner). Adam Bettcher/Getty Images

By the time the band arrived at the Blue Planet, the crowd was ravenous for the album they paid good money to experience. An adult man in my section excitedly screamed, “It’s the Blue Planet!” Cuomo lamented that the planet was dying. “We need the Blue Album to bring it back to life!” The crowd screamed. “That’s one small step for Weezer, one giant leap for Weezerkind!” _Another_ scream for this bad, unabashedly cornball line. Why? Because everybody knew that once Cuomo planted the Weezer flag into the Blue Planet (there was a literal prop flag), they would launch into “My Name Is Jonas.”

The Blue Album section of the show really highlighted just how much that record feels like a greatest hits album without skips. When Cuomo hit the climactic guitar solo in “Buddy Holly,” it was a triumph. “Say It Ain’t So” encouraged the unbridled scream-singing of a sea of humanity, and so did “Undone (The Sweater Song).” Outside all the pageantry, this is just a rock band that’s exceptional at playing their best-loved songs.

Related Content

[### Oasis’ Reunion Tour Was All About the Joy of Positive Masculinity](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/oasis-reunion-tour-essay-positive-masculinity-1235460198/)

And again, all of this happened after sets from two unbelievable live bands. Dinosaur Jr. kicked the show off with a tight 30 minutes. It definitely felt truncated, but Lou Barlow thrashed around more than anybody else who took the stage that night, screaming “Mountain Man,” from the band’s 1985 debut album. Sure, there weren’t many songs in their set, but the ones they did play were “Just Like Heaven” and “Freak Scene” and “Feel the Pain.”

With Dinosaur Jr. offering zero banter and Weezer only speaking in highly scripted narrative beats, the Flaming Lips were the perfect counterweight — loose, congenial, conversational. Wayne Coyne took a moment to tell the Saint Paul crowd about the time the band handed Prince’s bodyguard a stack of their CDs as a gift to the icon. “As we were backstage after he played, his bodyguard came up to us and he had the stack of CDs and he said, ‘Prince doesn’t want these,’” Coyne said, calling it the greatest diss in history.

The Oklahoma City band announced that they were recording that night’s set, which may explain why they began more gradually and subtly with “The Spark That Bled” and “Suddenly Everything Has Changed.” They built to their bubblier hits like “The Yeah Yeah Yeah Song” and “She Don’t Use Jelly,” though the undisputed highlight of their performance was a twinkling-then-raucous cover of Madonna’s “Borderline.” Since they weren’t the headliners, it wasn’t the most maximal Flaming Lips show that’s ever been thrown. But what they lacked in humans walking around in bubbles and confetti cannons, they made up for with giant inflatable robots, people dancing around as huge eyeballs, and lasers.

Their set ended with a special request from Weezer — that the Flaming Lips end their set each night with “Do You Realize??” beneath an inflatable rainbow. Wayne Coyne encouraged the crowd to take advantage of what he called a “built-in moment.” Church-style, he told the crowd to turn to their neighbor and express their love. “I love you, guy,” said a total stranger two seats down from me.

And it was a moment, a bit of emotional catharsis before the crowd got raucous and the headliners got silly. With the lights up before Weezer came out, huge sections of the crowd could be seen wearing blue shirts. Whether they’re making you cheer for the survival of a fictional planet, ripping through “Surf Wax America,” blasting the crowd with blue confetti and streamers, or just standing backstage while J Mascis shreds, Weezer seem hell-bent on making sure you get your money’s worth out of this tour.

 ![Image 2: Author Image](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/9a779c59aa65a254850ddf36f21928c454d87007f418b6865ce755e928ecb526?s=50&d=mm&r=g)By [Kat Sophia](https://www.independent.com/author/kaatshengmail-com/ "Posts by Kat Sophia")

“Beverly Hills, that’s where I want to be … rollin’ like a celebrity.”

Whenever Weezer’s “Beverly Hills” came on the radio when I was a kid, I would air guitar and drum in the backseat of the car as though my life depended on it. The way the band’s songs were recorded, it was hard not to. The brash, loud sounds of the live sounding instrumentation, the tastefully simple melodies, and their conversational lyrics were perfect sonic fodder for a little burgeoning music nerd. Through the airwaves, Weezer became a huge part of my childhood and love of bands. Their music dominated the ’90s with platinum records and chart success, with their rock/emo-meets-pop sound.

Not too far from The Hills themselves, I went to see Weezer at the new Intuit Dome in Inglewood this past week. Celebrating 30 years of the band’s iconic self-titled LP (a k a _The Blue Album_) on their _The Voyage to the Blue Planet_ tour, they created a show where (dressed as astronauts) they are on a mission throughout the set list to play _The Blue Album_ in full.

The show started with the stage set up with a rocket ship in the center, along with a giant screen behind them displaying space imagery. There was a countdown on the side screens, and once it hit zero, the ship lifted to show the band underneath. The band exploded into “Anonymous” as the crowd roared. They played a string of hits, including “Pork and Beans,” “Island in the Sun,” and “Beverly Hills.” During “Island in the Sun,” the audience screamed “hip, hip” along with the band, and during “Beverly Hills,” the lead singer and guitarist swayed in unison back and forth, beaming as they played in tandem with one another.

The band then played a string of cuts from their album _Pinkerton_ as they entered the Pinkerton Asteroid Belt, with highlights including “Pink Triangle,” “Across the Sea,” and “Why Bother?” After “Across the Sea,” the band then grabbed a blue flag and stuck it into the stage, announcing that they had found their way to the Blue Planet.

Weezer played the entire _Blue Album_ top to bottom, and the audience loved it. Most people around me knew every word, and each song was filled with raucous, joyous energy as audience members jumped with joy and clutched each other’s hands as they sang the words to each other, laughing. And there was blue everywhere: Streamers flew through the air, the seats all lit up blue, and the blue lights flashed across the venue. During fan favorite “Say It Ain’t So,” the band looked the most excited of the night, genuinely enjoying watching audience members scream along.

After “Buddy Holly,” lead singer Rivers Cuomo punched both fists into the air in excitement. And during “Undone — The Sweater Song,” the band dropped silent during the chorus, letting the audience take over. It elicited a huge response from the crowd, as fans beamed while singing, “If you want to destroy my sweater, hold this thread as I walk away. Watch me unravel, I’ll soon be naked, lying on the floor.”

Toward the end of the show, I turned around to see an ocean of middle-aged men mimicking the same drum solos I did as a kid. A united community of fans in their own private worlds, it was a celebration together of the music that we’ve explored inside ourselves; embodying each band member as if you were part of the group. I wondered how many other people were tapping into that same kid. It was a blast being her again for a night.

If you missed Weezer performing live in the area, you kind of get a second chance.  A Weezer Concert Film is set for release!  It’s a stop on their Voyage To The Blue Planet Tour.  Now, I reviewed the show I went to, but I have to reiterate a few things.

First off, yes, [Weezer](https://weezer.com/) plays the Blue Album (their debut) in its entirety.  And they knock it out of the park.  The guitar riffs, the harmonies, the slow build-ups.  It’s a sight to behold.  They also play a ton of fan favorites before getting into the Blue Album.

About The Weezer Concert Film
-----------------------------

Now, since you have a chance to see this concert streaming from your own home, I don’t want to ruin much.  I’ll just tell you that there’s a really cool story that takes place throughout the show.  Rivers Cuomo and the band head out on a space adventure. Let’s just say that throughout it, they go through other planets and galaxies and that’s where the “Other” songs come into play.

The concert footage was filmed at Boston’s TD Garden on September 10th.  They’ve made it into a full-fledged concert film which you can stream either October 13th or October 14th.  The tour’s not over yet, but I think this is so cool for fans who passed on tickets but ae kicking themselves for not going.  I almost didn’t.  My wife and I thought it was pretty expensive and it was tough to get seats.  [But after witnessing the whole show, I can tell you…..it was worth it](https://wdhafm.com/2024/09/16/weezers-30th-anniversary/)!

I think even from home you’ll get a  great experience and be able to follow the story.  Plus, the sound will most likely be better as I’m sure it will come from the mixing board.

Even if you’re a passive Weezer fan I highly recommend this.  It’s a really fun experience!

It’s A Linkin Park Special Event On YouTube This Thursday
---------------------------------------------------------

We saw the [**Linkin Park countdown**](https://wdhafm.com/2024/08/26/linkin-park-timer-counting-down/) and then counted up. And now we are waiting for a Linkin Park special event on YouTube This Thursday.

The event will take place at 6pm EST on Youtube Thursday. More waiting , I know, but at least we know something is definitely coming. Or at least we think!

I was hoping that Linkin Park would be announcing either a tour with rotating vocalists or maybe even an album of new music starring guest vocalists throughout the album.  I thought that would be something really fun and not take away from Chester Bennington’s legacy.

A tour would be fun to see the rest of the band.  They are super talented and play so well live.  I thought it’d be cool to have a tour with revolving singers at different locations or something like that.  [An album of new music](https://wdhafm.com/listicle/new-music-releases-to-be-excited-for/) would be tremendous as well, however instead of announcing one new singer, I thought they could just have different guests on each track.

What makes [Linkin Park](https://xn--pda.linkinpark.com/) so special is their ability to craft songs that are all over the map sound and no two songs sound alike.  There’s always a unique spin and they could go from ballad to in-your-face, loud, and heavy guitars in a matter of minutes.  But of course, to me, the band was and always will be Chester Bennington.  His voice was so extraordinary.  He went from melodic, soft singing to near screams in just seconds.  And live, he always sounded flawless.

The Linkin Park sound couldn’t be defined.  It had elements of hip hop sure, but it was straight-up hard rock at moments - trippy, experimental tribal anthem the next.  You really got a good mix that was so interesting!

BREAKING THE HABIT
------------------

What a cool, interesting vibe. It's got a lot going on in this tune, with some cool drums and a relatable lyrical theme from Chester. Really cool stuff!

MY DECEMBER
-----------

Such a dark sounding song.  Yet it's hopeful and intriguing, and emotional all at once.  A real masetrpiece.

WAITING FOR THE END
-------------------

This one pumps me up.  From the album that left fans divided "A Thousand Suns".  There's no denying that this song is filled with hope and passion in Chester's voice.

LIES GREED MISERY
-----------------

This is really a rare example of hip hop - metal.  It's got elements from both genres and is so angst ridden, that it fuels and pumps you up.  Such great screams towards the end!

SHADOW OF THE DAY
-----------------

A really nice ballad that just has a lot of heart and emotion.  Really a cool laid back vibe with a nice melodic hook!

A space shuttle sat center stage at TD Garden on Sept. 10, directly beneath a giant blue “W.” Circular screens flanking the spectacle displayed “five minutes until lift-off.” The clock ticked down — accompanied by the shouts of a packed arena of fans — to the sparks and f0g machine-induced smoke of an explosive takeoff. As the ship lifted into the sky, Weezer took the stage and kicked off the show with “II. Anonymous,” an astronomical start to their space-themed “Voyage to the Blue Planet” tour.

This introduction, which came complete with a video introducing the interstellar plot of the concert, set the tone for the next hour and 40 minutes: Lighthearted, fantastical, and absolutely unrelenting.

![Image 1](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/230729_1372778.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

The curated setlist was one of the performance’s many strengths. Weezer performed a wide cross-section of their songs from the heavier “Hash Pipe” to mellow “Island in the Sun,” with even the pensive “Any Friend of Diane’s” making the cut for the first section of the concert, which underscored their ascent through the stars in pursuit of the titular “Blue Planet.” In many ways, the first part of the setlist felt as though it had been directly picked by fans themselves, which is unsurprising given the “Setlist Survey” link on [the lead singer and guitarist's website](https://riverscuomo.com/home).

The vibrational hodgepodge was kept afloat by a stellar vocal and instrumental evening for the band. Lead vocals from Rivers Cuomo ’06 sported a clean and straight-off-the-album sound that added to the faithfulness of the performance without subtracting from artistic value. Guitarist and backup vocalist Brian Bell, bassist and backup vocalist Scott Shriner, and drummer Patrick Wilson were similarly at their best. Taking essentially no break between songs, the musicians delivered nonstop excellence.

![Image 2](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/230810_1372779.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

Weezer Concert Review 2024 Image 3 -

![Image 3](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/230910_1372780.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

Weezer Concert Review 2024 Image 4 -

![Image 4](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/231034_1372781.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

Weezer Concert Review 2024 Image 5 -

The narrative and extravagant set of the concert drove the energy of this lengthy homage to Weezer’s incredible discography. The stage, covered in large asteroids, lights, and backed by a huge screen displaying zany cosmic imagery, took advantage of the large, open space at TD Garden.

During “Perfect Situation,” narrative and showmanship cohered, as planets descended from the ceiling over the stage while the screen displayed a battle between the alien “Bokkus” and the protagonist space shuttle. Serving as the main antagonist of the concert and primary plot agent of the voyage, Bokkus is himself a throwback to Weezer’s glory days as the mysterious brain-child of Wilson.

Shot down by Bokkus and crash landing in the “Pinkerton Asteroid Belt,” this provided the perfect segue into a brief selection of five songs from the album “Pinkerton,” including favorites like “Getchoo,” “Why Bother?,” and “Pink Triangle,” which brought much-needed rock energy to the stage as the audience prepared for the main event — landing on the “Blue Planet” for Weezer’s performance of the entire “Weezer” album, also known as the Blue Album.

![Image 5](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/231130_1372782.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

This final segment — complete with a final battle with Bokkus and Cuomo-shaped aliens known as “Weezoids” — was a pleasurable assault on the senses. Engaging visuals and a sincere demeanor from the performers made up for their otherwise stiff disposition on stage. Upon “landing,” the band re-entered, placing a W-shaped flag on the “Blue Planet.”

“One small step for Weezer, one giant leap for Weezerkind,” said Cuomo in the moments leading up to “My Name is Jonas,” the song that kicked off the Blue Album performance.

![Image 6](https://thumbnails.thecrimson.com/photos/2024/09/16/231223_1372783.jpg.1500x1000_q95_crop-smart_upscale.jpg)

The last moments of the concert brought out some of Weezer’s best musical work, including mind-blowing instrumental interludes from Shriner and Bell. Every note burst with a musical integrity and intensity that only a return to the Blue Album could offer. The band went all-out in tribute to their debut and, arguably, apotheosis.

Several crowd-surfers and a mosh pit demonstrated the buzz of the audience. Cuomo remarked that was the first time he’s ever seen anyone mosh to “Only in Dreams,” a hit that closed the concert with all the pomp and blue-confetti one could expect from the evening.

The lead singer summarized it best.

“What a voyage!” said Cuomo.

Weezer to debut live movie ‘Weezer’s Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film’
=================================================================================

 2024-10-11 [Rock Daypop](https://www.frankvermont.com/category/rock-daypop/)[Leave a reply](https://www.frankvermont.com/weezer-to-debut-live-movie-weezers-voyage-to-the-blue-planet-the-concert-film/#respond)

![Image 11: Rivers Cuomo of Weezer preforming at Pine Knob Music Theater. Clarkston^ MI - June 18 2023](https://dehayf5mhw1h7.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/709/2024/10/11083034/shutterstock_2320414623665364-250x250.webp)

Weezer have announced a concert film shot during their ongoing 2024 tour celebrating the 30th anniversary of their self-titled debut, aka _The Blue Album._

Titled [_Weezer’s Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film_](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/weezer-releasing-live-movie-voyage-to-the-blue-planet-concert-film-1235786666/), it was captured at Boston’s TD Garden on September 10th and will livestream at [Moment.co](http://moment.co/weezer) on October 13th and 14th.

The band posted on [social media](https://x.com/Weezer/status/1839350385607139720): _“One small step for man, one giant leap for Weezerkind ![Image 12: 🚀](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/15.0.3/72x72/1f680.png) On October 13th + 14th, we’re bringing you a very special concert film of The Voyage to the Blue Planet Tour (shot at the Boston show). For all of you that couldn’t make it out to the tour, now’s your chance to come celebrate 30 years of the Blue Album with us! Grab your popcorn ![Image 13: 🍿](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/15.0.3/72x72/1f37f.png) and your early bird tickets on @momentworld ’til 12pm PT tomorrow, and see you on October 13th + 14th http://moment.co/weezer”_

Weezer are also celebrating the Blue Album’s 30th anniversary with an expansive reissue featuring 36 unreleased tracks. [Pre-orders are ongoing](http://weezer.lnk.to/blue30?utm_campaign=The%20Blue%20Album%2030th%20Anniversary%20Edition&utm_medium=Link-in-bio&utm_source=Beacons) ahead of its release on November 1st.
